text: This case study is a fictional, illustrative scenario built to teach a real decision pattern, not a report of an actual company. During an authorized assessment of a fictional healthcare network's patient-portal infrastructure, a tester finds something that puts real pressure on every methodology lesson this chapter has covered.

Deep into scanning, Priya finds a legacy claims-processing system reachable from the in-scope network, but never listed in the original scope document. Everyone assumed it was basically decommissioned. It is not -- it processes real claims daily, and a careful check reveals an authentication bypass that would let an unauthenticated user view other patients' claims data. Once the client's leadership hears about it, the pushback isn't a request to hide the finding outright. It's softer: downgrade the severity, call it out of scope, leave it for a future engagement.

The whole situation hinges on keeping two separate questions apart. Whether the system was in the original scope document is a scoping fact, and business pressure can legitimately affect how that gets documented. How severe the authentication bypass actually is, is a completely different, technical fact -- and no amount of budget pressure or contract-renewal politics is allowed to touch that number.

The professional path runs through Lesson 1's documented escalation channel instead of an informal email thread with an unhappy VP. The finding gets reported as an out-of-scope discovery and still flagged at full Critical severity -- one doesn't cancel the other. The client gets offered a plain-language executive conversation about the real business risk, using Lesson 30's executive-summary skill in a harder meeting than usual. And if anyone asks for the finding to be deleted outright, that request gets declined, in writing, because a tester's integrity to the findings outranks a client's comfort with them.

Pushback like this isn't rare, and it's rarely hostile -- it's usually budget pressure or a sincere belief that a system was already gone. The real test of a professional pentester isn't whether they can find vulnerabilities; it's whether the report that leaves the building still says what the testing actually found. Lesson 32 closes this capstone chapter by tracing that same discipline back through all eight chapters of this course.
